blocks.content: Imagine you are ordering a pizza. You call the place, the cashier takes your order, passes it to the kitchen, the chef starts cooking, and eventually someone arrives at your door with the food.
Every step happens in a fixed order. Each person waits for the previous one to finish before doing their part.
That is exactly what a Sequence Diagram shows in software.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245793265-204b1851.png
If you want full color control on participant boxes, the best option would be an HTML artifact instead. Want me to build that?
1. What is a Sequence Diagram?
A sequence diagram is a UML diagram that shows how different parts of a system talk to each other to get something done.
It focuses on three things who the participants are, what messages they exchange, and in what order those messages happen.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: "Who does what, and when?"
Why Sequence Diagrams Matter
1. See runtime behavior at a glance
Code execution jumps across classes, services, and layers. A sequence diagram puts the entire flow on one page every call, every response, every handoff without reading a single line of code.
2. Debug complex flows faster

When something breaks in production you need to know the exact order of events. Did the payment fire before the inventory was reserved? Did the notification go out before the order was confirmed? Sequence diagrams make these flows impossible to misread.
3. Bridge the gap between requirements and code

A use case diagram says "the customer can place an order." A class diagram shows which classes exist. Neither one tells you the exact sequence of calls that makes it happen. Sequence diagrams fill that gap.
2. Building Blocks of a Sequence Diagram
blocks.text: 2. Building Blocks of a Sequence Diagram

blocks.content: Every sequence diagram is built from four elements. Understand these and you can read any diagram you come across.
Actors and Participants
An actor is an outside entity that kicks off the interaction a user, an external system. A participant is an internal component that does the actual work a service, a controller, a database.
The distinction is simple: actors trigger from outside, participants handle it on the inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245793631-31e45c84.png
Customer
sits on the far left because they start the interaction. The three internal components handle everything after that.
Lifelines

The dashed vertical line dropping down from each participant is called a lifeline. It represents time moving forward top is earlier, bottom is later. Every message arrow connects one lifeline to another, pinning each interaction to an exact point in the sequence.
Activation Bars
When a participant is actively doing something running a method, waiting for a reply
AuthService stays active the entire time it is waiting on the database. Database has its own shorter bar nested inside. Without these bars you cannot tell who is busy and who is just sitting idle.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245794146-31718ff8.png
Messages

Messages are the horizontal arrows between lifelines. Each one is labeled with what is being sent usually a method name with its parameters. The arrow points from sender to receiver. The style of the arrow tells you what kind of message it is and that is exactly what the next section covers.
3. Types of Messages in Sequence Diagrams
blocks.text: 3. Types of Messages in Sequence Diagrams

blocks.content: Messages are what bring a sequence diagram to life. Each type has a different arrow style that tells you something specific about how the sender and receiver interact.
There are six types to know.
1. Synchronous Messages
Like a phone call. You dial, someone picks up, and you wait on the line until they finish and respond. The sender is completely blocked until the receiver sends something back.
Solid line with a filled arrowhead. The most common type most method calls in OOP are synchronous.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245794406-e8c7360e.png
Follow the flow every caller waits. The database replies to OrderService, which replies to OrderController, which replies to the User. Each one blocked until the one below it finishes.
2. Asynchronous Messages
Like sending a text. You fire it off and keep moving. No waiting, no blocking, sometimes no reply at all.
Solid line with an open arrowhead. Used for queuing jobs, publishing events, firing notifications.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245794887-f43ff3d4.png
OrderService drops the event and moves on immediately. It does not hang around waiting for the email to go out. The queue handles delivery on its own time.
3. Return Messages
The response to a synchronous call. Data flowing back from receiver to sender.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245795176-abc5e8f0.png
Dashed line with an open arrowhead. Every -->> arrow in the diagrams above is a return message.
Technically optional in UML but always worth including. They make the diagram self-explanatory you can see exactly what each component hands back without guessing.
4. Self Messages
When an object calls one of its own methods. The arrow loops back to the same lifeline.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245795643-ce2bf46c.png
Common for internal validation, helper methods, or business rule checks. The looping arrow makes it visually clear no external call is happening here.
5. Create Messages
Shows that a new object is being instantiated mid-flow. The new participant does not exist at the top of the diagram it appears at the exact point it is created.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245795886-176d97f6.png
Invoice is not there from the start. It appears only when OrderService creates it after the order is validated. This communicates clearly that invoices are born dynamically, not pre-existing objects.
6. Destroy Messages
Marks the point where an object ceases to exist. Shown with an X at the end of the destroyed participant's lifeline.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245796375-1be06e5e.png

AfterOrderServiceclears it, theCartis gone. The X signals that this object no longer exists from this point forward. Useful any time you need to show cleanup clearing carts, closing sessions, releasing locks.
4. Combined Fragments

Straight-line diagrams only tell half the story. Real systems make decisions, repeat steps, skip things, and run tasks at the same time. Combined fragments are how you show all of that inside a sequence diagram.
Each one is a box drawn over part of the diagram with a keyword in the top left corner that tells you what kind of logic is happening inside.
alt / else (If This, Else That)

The alt fragment is your if/else block. It splits into two or more sections separated by a dashed line. Each section carries a condition in square brackets and only the matching one actually executes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245796795-95291a87.png
Two outcomes, one diagram. Payment goes through user gets a success. Payment bounces user gets an error. No need to draw two separate diagrams for the same flow.
loop (Run It Again)
The loop fragment wraps a block that repeats as long as a condition stays true. It maps directly to a for or while loop in your code.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245797162-07e70caf.png
Every item in the order gets a stock check before anything moves forward. The loop box wraps the whole thing so you know immediately this block repeats once for each item, not just once total.
opt (Maybe, Maybe Not)
The opt fragment is a single conditional block with no fallback. If the condition is met the block runs. If not the diagram skips right past it. Think of it as an if with no else attached.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245797400-501a609d.png
Customers who bring a promo code get it validated. Everyone else skips straight to the confirmation. The opt box makes that optional step visible without adding a redundant empty branch.
par (All at Once)
The par fragment is for tasks that run side by side at the same time. Each section inside fires concurrently  not one after another.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245797696-d5194cd1.png

The second an order lands, three things kick off in parallel confirmation email goes out, stock gets locked, and the event gets logged. Theparblock makes it crystal clear these are not queued up one behind the other. They all start at the same moment.
